answer: Full B3 run completed and all nine required artifacts written and validated. Model: 2D Ising nonconserved Metropolis (Glauber) kinetics at T = control = 2.0236 (< Tc = 2.26918), periodic boundaries, checkerboard-vectorized sweeps, numpy default_rng(dynamics_seed) created exactly once, 12,305 sweeps (~7 s CPU). Key scientific finding: at this T (0.89 Tc) the finite 100x100 system coarsens for t <~ 500 sweeps and then equilibrates into the ordered phase (|m| -> ~0.90 ~ Onsager m_eq = 0.912; wall density -> plateau rho_eq = 0.0687 set by equilibrium thermal droplet fluctuations); the requested snapshot schedule extends 4 decades beyond equilibration. Diagnostics were therefore designed around a data-defined coarsening window: L(t) = 1/rho(t) fit L = A t^alpha over t in [5, 502] gives alpha = 0.1550 +/- 0.0039, amplitude 5.204, r^2 = 0.9453; the Family-Vicsek collapse of the connected normalized correlation (C-m^2)/(1-m^2) vs r/L restricted to growth-window snapshots {10, 41, 172} gives quality 0.775 (relative RMS spread 0.2248, x-range [0, 4.2385]). All arrays are float64, finite, and exactly the required shapes; both JSONs have exactly the required keys (collapse_dimension = 2, collapse_grid_size = 100); figure.png (valid 1560x1230 PNG) shows state snapshots, C(r,t), the collapse, the L(t) fit, and both series; the run is byte-for-byte reproducible. Note: matplotlib is not installed in this sandbox and network is blocked, so simulation.py imports matplotlib lazily and falls back to a self-contained numpy+stdlib PNG renderer; in a matplotlib-equipped runtime it uses matplotlib automatically.
